title: The name Waheguru
hook: the name used by the Bhatts in their verses praising the Gurus (Swayye, ang 1402)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the names of God in the Granth: Hari, Ram, Gobind, Allah, Khuda and more. Your line was many names. Whose word for God did you hear, and did it feel like a door? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

Wah. A sound people make without deciding to. A sunset over the fields. A baby's first step. A friend's voice on the phone after years. Wah slips out before any proper sentence can. Now take that sound and set it right in front of the word Guru. Waheguru. It's the name Sikhs repeat in simran, the word that closes the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, the name a congregation says together as a reading ends. Yesterday's crowd of names has one at its center for Sikhs, and this is it. And in the Granth itself it turns up somewhere a newcomer might not look: near the end of the book, in the voices of poets.
screen: `WAH: THE SOUND OF WONDER.` → `WAH + GURU.` → `IN THE VOICES OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Begin with the poets. Close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib come the Swayye of the Bhatts, verses by bards who praised the Gurus. Tradition remembers them as poets who came to the Guru's court and sang what they saw. Their verses sit in the same scripture as the Gurus' own hymns. Now the name in their mouths. Around Ang fourteen hundred and two, in a verse praising Guru Ram Das, a Bhatt named Gayand breaks again and again into one cry: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru. It reads less like a definition and more like someone who can't stop saying it. What does the name hold? Sikhs explain it as wonder joined to Guru: wah, the cry of astonishment, and Guru, the one who brings light and teaching. Put together, something like wonderful Lord. Notice what kind of name that is. Yesterday, Guru Arjan said our names describe God's deeds. Waheguru doesn't describe a deed. It describes what happens to the one who notices. It's a name that is mostly a gasp. And then, where the gasp went. From poets' verses it became the center of daily life. Sikhs repeat it in simran, slowly or quickly, aloud or under the breath. It is the word in the Khalsa greeting. Sikhs call it gurmantar, the Guru's own word to repeat. A name that began as praise in a bard's song is now said in kitchens, cars and hospital rooms. Wonderful Lord.
screen: `THE BHATTS: BARDS IN THE GRANTH.` · `GAYAND: WAHEGURU, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `WAH, WONDER, JOINED TO GURU.` · `FROM A BARD'S SONG TO DAILY SIMRAN.` · then, large: `WONDERFUL LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Waheguru slowly. Settle, and breathe. On the out-breath, let the name come out at walking pace: wah, then he, then guru. If you'd rather not say it, simply say wah, the sound of wonder, and think of one thing today that deserves it. Let the word stretch. Let the pause after it stretch too. If your mind runs off, bring it back with the next wah. The bell holds the time.
The name Waheguru. Wonder joined to Guru: the name the Bhatts cried out in their verses, and the name Sikhs repeat in simran today. Today's word.
Your line: wonderful lord. Today, the next time wah slips out of you, at a view or a kindness, stop and let it last one breath longer. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, alone or together, and use it in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; congregations often say it aloud at the end of a reading.
